## Backup: the contract in full {#b-endpoints data-section="7"}

::: {style="font-size:0.96em;"}
| **Endpoint** | **Purpose** |
|:------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------|
| `POST /api/v1/sessions` | create a solver session, fresh or from a restart |
| `POST /api/v1/sessions/:id/advance` | integrate the physics forward by *dt*; return the full state |
| `POST /api/v1/sessions/:id/intervene` | apply operator actions as index and value pairs |
| `POST /api/v1/sessions/:id/checkpoint` | snapshot the solver state; return a checkpoint identifier |
| `POST /api/v1/sessions/:id/restore` | rewind the session to a prior checkpoint |
| `DELETE /api/v1/sessions/:id` | destroy the session and free its resources |
| `GET /api/v1/sessions/:id/state` | the current state, without advancing time |
| `GET /api/v1/health` | liveness check |
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.72em; margin-top:0.6em;"}
- **`AdvanceResponse`**: five arrays and nothing domain-specific: volumes,
  junctions, control variables, variable trips, logical trips.
- **Trips** are threshold comparisons evaluated every time step; they fire
  once and latch. The engine derives pivotal events from trip firings.
- **`ParameterMapper`**, on the solver side, packs native state into the wire
  format: adding a domain means writing a solver service and its mapper.
:::

## Backup: the solver interface inside the engine {#b-solver-code data-section="7"}

![](figs/tikz/solver-decoupling.svg){fig-align="center" width="94%"}

::: {style="font-size:0.82em; margin-top:0.5em;"}
- Everything above the interface (the tree, the crew, the dispatcher, the
  checkpoints) runs identically over either implementation: the engine cannot
  tell a binary restart image from a checkpoint id.
- A callback interface returns control to the PRA core at branching and
  evaluation points, so crew-model branching is the same whichever solver
  supplies the physics.
- A standalone mock PWR server (310 parameters, the same contract) runs the
  full dynamic event tree with no Fortran, serial and under MPI.
:::

## Backup: where this sits among dynamic PRA tools {#b-peer-tools data-section="7"}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](figs/tikz/platform-map.svg){fig-align="center" width="100%"}
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
::: {style="font-size:0.74em;"}
- **ADAPT** drives severe-accident codes through a scheduler and is
  simulator-neutral by design
- **RAVEN** is a general sampling and dynamic event tree framework around
  codes
- **MCDET** combines Monte Carlo with discrete dynamic event trees
- **EMRALD** couples state-machine models to external simulations
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.78em; margin-top:0.7em;"}
Simulator neutrality is not new. What differs here is the **form of the
coupling**: a documented service contract, in-memory state exchange and typed
branching semantics, [with parallel traversal and crew cognition in one
platform.]{style="color:#B40000;"}
:::
:::
::::

::: {.slideref}
Hakobyan et al., *Nucl. Eng. Des.* **238** (2008); Alfonsi et al., RAVEN Theory Manual, INL/EXT-16-38178; Kloos and Peschke, *Nucl. Sci. Eng.* **153** (2006); Prescott et al., PSAM 14 (2018). The map is the dissertation's; it also places DETAM and HUNTER.
:::

## Backup: three baselines, and how speedup is counted {#b-baselines data-section="7"}

```{=html}
<div class="xcards">
  <div class="xcard">
    <div class="x-name">Original behavior</div>
    <div class="x-how">the reference engine as it ran: no property caching, restart on disk</div>
  </div>
  <div class="xcard">
    <div class="x-name">Optimized serial</div>
    <div class="x-how">property caching and in-memory restart, one sequence at a time</div>
  </div>
  <div class="xcard">
    <div class="x-name">Parallel</div>
    <div class="x-how">measured against the optimized serial run, on the same platform and build</div>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: {style="font-size:0.8em; margin-top:0.6em;"}
$$S_n = \frac{T_1}{T_n}, \qquad E_n = \frac{S_n}{n-1}$$

with $n-1$ counting workers: rank 0 schedules and never runs physics, so
useful parallelism starts at three ranks.
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.72em; margin-top:0.4em;"}
Platforms: an 8-core Linux x86_64 host and a 14-core Apple-silicon ARM64
host; Intel, GNU and Clang toolchains. Optimizations unrelated to parallelism
would otherwise inflate every speedup.
:::

## Backup: measured performance, the paper's summary {#b-perf-table data-section="7"}

::: {style="font-size:1.05em;"}
| **Effect** | **Configuration** | **Result** |
|:--------------------------|:---------------------------------------|:---------------------------|
| serial optimizations alone | same build, *T* = 100 s | 3.9× |
| MPI, 8-core Linux | GNU Release, *n* = 4, against optimized serial | 2.1 to 2.3× |
| MPI, 14-core ARM64 | *n* = 10 to 12, against optimized serial | up to about 4.5× |
| modern toolchain | gfortran `-O3` against the reference Intel path | 2 to 2.5× |
| LZ4 queue compression | restart buffers; runs at high rank counts | about 3× smaller; peak memory down by up to 30% |
| composite | best (ARM64, *n* = 10, compressed) against the original | 156× (752 s to 4.8 s) |
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.72em; margin-top:0.6em;"}
- Property caching removes a steam-table reload of about 6.3 s per sequence
  (to about 0.024 s); in-memory restart removes tens of MB of disk I/O per
  branch.
- At *T* = 200 s and *n* = 8 on the ARM64 host, compression takes peak
  residency from 3.7 GB to 2.6 GB.
- Live monitoring, an HTTP view of the growing tree served from rank 0,
  measures within run-to-run variance even at 883 sequences.
:::

## Backup: laptop wall times, rank by rank {#b-wall-times data-section="7"}

::: {style="font-size:1.05em;"}
| | ***T* = 100 s**, default | ***T* = 100 s**, LZ4 queue | ***T* = 200 s**, default | ***T* = 200 s**, LZ4 queue |
|:------------------|--------:|--------:|--------:|--------:|
| serial, optimized | 21.4 s | | 60.7 s | |
| *n* = 4 | 11.4 s | 10.4 s | 31.7 s | 31.5 s |
| *n* = 8 | 7.4 s | 5.7 s | 16.8 s | 14.9 s |
| *n* = 10 | 5.8 s | **4.8 s** | 19.0 s | 14.7 s |
| *n* = 11 | | 4.8 s | | **13.4 s** |
| *n* = 12 | 5.0 s | | 18.8 s | |
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.72em; margin-top:0.6em;"}
- Speedup levels off near *n* = 10 to 12, where the tree runs out of usable
  width, not where the machine does.
- Compression pays at high rank counts: less resident restart data per rank,
  and messages three times smaller outweigh the cost of compressing them.
- Efficiency declines with rank count as the serial fraction (the root
  sequence and the scheduling overhead) asserts itself; larger trees sustain
  it further.
:::

::: {.slideref}
14-core ARM64 laptop, same platform and build; generic three-loop PWR benchmark. A speedup is the serial time of its horizon divided by an entry of this table; empty cells are not in the paper's data.
:::

budget.]{style="color:#B40000;"}
:::

## Backup: one core against six workers {#anim-mpi-dispatch data-section="7" background-iframe="assets/anim/362-mpi-dispatch.html" background-interactive="true" visibility="uncounted" .no-band}

::: {.notes}
[Plays about eighteen seconds and freezes; Replay bottom right; PageDown moves
on.]

The same tree twice, side by side. On the left, one core runs one sequence at
a time, and every new branch waits its turn in the queue. On the right, a
worker keeps its own transient past the branch point, and the new branch goes
to a free worker at once, or waits in the server's queue. The wall time is the
queue's, and how full the queue is, the tree decides.
:::

## Backup: serialization, live state to bytes and back to life {#anim-serialization data-section="7" background-iframe="assets/anim/serialization-animation.html" background-interactive="true" visibility="uncounted" .no-band}

::: {.notes}
[Plays about twenty-seven seconds and freezes; Replay bottom right; PageDown
moves on.]

For a branch to move between workers, the live state of a simulation has to
travel. On the left is that state at a branch point: a web of objects, not a
table. Serialization walks the web: each class writes its own fields, every
pointer is followed, an object already written becomes a back-reference, and
the solver's restart image rides along as bytes. The receiver rebuilds the
same web. The identical archive path also writes checkpoint files, so one
round-trip test suite anchors both.
:::

## Backup: checkpoint and resume, regression-tested {#b-resume data-section="7"}

::: {style="font-size:0.92em;"}
| **permutation** | **what it proves** |
|:---|:---|
| serial to serial; MPI to MPI | checkpoint and resume in place |
| serial to MPI; MPI to serial | the checkpoint is neutral to the execution mode |
| MPI on 3 ranks to 5; on 5 ranks to 3 | the rank count is chosen at resume time |
| compressed queue to serial | compression state survives the crossing |
| file-backed restart data, 3 ranks to 4 | restart data held on disk embeds correctly |
| interrupt in mid-run, then resume | the on-the-fly path equals the planned one |
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.74em; margin-top:0.6em;"}
- Each permutation must reproduce the reference sequence counts exactly.
- A checkpoint holds the task queue, the held branch data and the
  completed-sequence records, LZ4-compressed and fingerprinted by version and
  configuration.
- On the cluster: checkpointed on 2 nodes and 64 ranks, resumed in a separate
  allocation on 4 nodes and 128 ranks, with the end states of the straight
  run reproduced identically.
:::

## Backup: the rank ladder on the 35k tree {#b-ladder data-section="7"}

![](figs/large_tree_ladder.svg){fig-align="center" width="84%"}

::: {style="font-size:0.78em;"}
The tree phase follows the ideal 1/N line up to 768 ranks: 98 and 95% on the
Intel nodes at 128 and 256 ranks, counted from 32, and 98 and 94% on the AMD
nodes at 512 and 768, counted from 256.
The tail (merge and extraction) is 4 to 24 minutes under a tree phase of
27 minutes to 15 hours.
:::

::: {.slideref}
A. Tezbasaran, Ph.D. dissertation, NC State University (2026), Chapter 3. The designed tree of about 35,000 sequences, mission 3,600 s, on NC State's Hazel cluster.
:::
